extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, DHS/USCIS adjudicators, policy stakeholders, and commenters on public charge rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for making public charge inadmissibility determinations (what benefits count, evidence collection, denial writing, bonds, data collection, exemptions, and use of empirical data). Intended to guide USCIS officers and inform stakeholders commenting on or complying with the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis — individual, not household
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'household' is not the proper unit of analysis when examining public benefits use, particularly for households with a mixture of U.S. citizens, naturalized/derived citizens, and noncitizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS rejects approaches that attribute all benefit use by dependents or other household members to a noncitizen applicant (the 'household' approach). Analyses that look only at the education level of the head of household rather than the education of the person receiving benefits are insufficient to attribute benefit use to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weight of education and income must be empirically justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged giving significant weight to education and income as predictors that a noncitizen will become a public charge; DHS requires empirical support before treating education or income as primary predictors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the cited analysis did not provide quantitative evidence linking income to benefit use nor compare education/income to other statutory factors (age, health, skills, assets/resources). Evidence should inform the analysis; DHS may issue guidance based on empirical analysis of best-available data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical analysis and best-available data for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may periodically issue guidance to officers that considers how statutory factors affect the likelihood a noncitizen will become a public charge based on empirical analysis of the best-available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will rely on internal economists and may engage external experts and the public; empirical analyses should be appropriate and supported by available data. Guidance may be adjusted in response to new data and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection limitations and ELIS transition
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS adjudicative systems currently do not allow comprehensive automated collection of public charge denial data without manual review; CLAIMS3 lacks some tracking fields (e.g., race/ethnicity), while ELIS allows indicating '212(a)(4) Public Charge' as a denial reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once all adjustment of status application varieties are transitioned into ELIS, DHS expects to be able to more easily analyze denial data for disproportionate impacts and share with external analysts as appropriate, consistent with law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit subject-matter expert input for factor-specific analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of specific statutory factors (e.g., health) should include perspectives of experts in those fields (e.g., medical researchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may use internal economists and civil surgeons (for medical info from Form I-693) and may engage external scientific collaborators where appropriate; DHS solicited and will consider external comment and data during rulemaking and guidance development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude benefits received while in an exempt immigration category
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will prohibit considering any public benefits received by a noncitizen during periods in which the noncitizen was present in an immigration category that is exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility or for which the noncitizen received a waiver of public charge inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion is reflected in proposed 8 CFR 212.23(a) / 212.23(c). DHS reasons Congress intended vulnerable exempt categories to receive benefits without adverse immigration consequences; treating those benefits as disqualifying would undermine that intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — cash assistance or long-term institutionalization before/after exempt status counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense received prior to or subsequent to being in an exempt status will be considered in a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits received while actually in an exempt category are excluded, but cash assistance/long-term institutionalization outside those exempt periods remain countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expand statutory exemptions beyond Congress's list
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not expand the exemption-from-consideration to additional populations (e.g., withholding of removal, DED, deferred action, general parolees) that Congress did not expressly exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS limits exclusions to the categories Congress chose; commenters' requests to expand exemptions were declined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refugee-benefits exclusion (including certain non-refugee beneficiaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider public benefits received by those granted refugee benefits (eligible for resettlement assistance, entitlement programs, and other benefits) when making public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exemption applies to categories eligible for all three types of refugee support and is extended to certain populations Congress intended to protect (e.g., Afghan allies resettled under Operation Allies Welcome and trafficking victims). DHS encourages these populations to access services without fear of immigration consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written denial decisions must articulate consideration of each statutory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Every written denial decision issued by USCIS should reflect consideration of each of the factors outlined in the rule and specifically articulate the reasons for the officer's determination (including the affidavit of support where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes this requirement promotes fairness, transparency, and consistency. The rule adds the requirement that officers include a discussion of each statutory factor in the already-required written denial decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and public access to denial records
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not establish a mechanism for the public to request all denials related to adjustment-of-status public charge denials (via FOIA or otherwise) due to privacy implications and potential administrative burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not broadly public, once data systems permit (ELIS), DHS may analyze and potentially share data with external analysts to the extent appropriate and consistent with law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language requirement for denial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial decisions should be clear and easy to read, consistent with the Plain Writing Act of 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS has an internal plain language program; denial decisions follow USCIS plain language policies and include citations to relevant law or courts to support decisions. Commenters' suggestions for Easy Read formats are acknowledged but USCIS follows its existing plain language program.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to write explanations for approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not require officers to issue written analyses explaining each factor in all cases where the officer determines that an applicant is not inadmissible under the public charge ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring written explanations for approvals would be burdensome and inconsistent with USCIS practice for other grounds of inadmissibility; the existing long-standing requirement to write reasons for denials remains unchanged except to add factor discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-485 will collect targeted public-charge information
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will add several questions to Form I-485 to collect public-charge-related information not previously on the form: household size, income, assets, liabilities, applicant's education or skills, use of TANF or SSI, and any long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants not subject to the public charge ground will be able to skip related questions. Open-ended narrative questions were converted to multiple-choice to reduce time burden. Additional space is available if applicants need to provide more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit questions to benefits that will be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not ask overly broad questions about 'any public assistance'; additional questions are limited to the use of benefits that would be considered in a public charge determination: TANF; SSI; State/Tribal/territorial/local cash benefit programs for income maintenance; and long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the variety of noncash programs, DHS will issue future guidance with examples of widely used noncash programs (e.g., SNAP, CHIP, Medicaid) but will not exhaustively list them on the form or instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include exhaustive exemption list on Form I-485 instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declined to include the full list of noncitizens exempt from section 212(a)(4) in Form I-485 instructions (29 classes in new 8 CFR 212.23) to avoid imposing burden on all applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full list is included in the regulations and DHS will include a list of exemptions within sub-regulatory guidance instead of the form instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support forms unchanged; no I-485 supplement
rubrics_metrics.description: No changes to Form I-864 or I-864A were proposed; these continue to collect sponsor/household size, income, and assets and do not collect intending immigrant information. DHS decided not to create a supplement to Form I-485.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS concluded that creating a supplement would increase burden for applicants and the agency; Form I-485 will sufficiently collect needed public charge-related information and a skip question reduces burden on inapplicable applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Requests for Evidence (RFE) before denying for insufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS policy instructs officers to issue Requests for Evidence in cases involving insufficient evidence before denying such cases unless the officer determines there is no possibility the applicant could overcome a finding of ineligibility by submitting additional evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural requirement is intended to reduce incorrect denials based on insufficient documentary record.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor dispositive except lack of required Affidavit of Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge inadmissibility determinations are based on the totality of circumstances; no one factor described in the rule should be the sole criterion for determining likelihood of becoming a public charge other than the lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support, if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers must consider all statutory factors (including age, health, assets/resources, education/skills, and affidavit of support) and contextualize temporary issues where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum public charge bond amount and bond purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not permit negligible bonds (e.g., $100) to overcome public charge inadmissibility; the minimum bond amount DHS will set is $1,000 to ensure governments are held harmless against the noncitizen becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under section 213 of the INA, DHS may admit a noncitizen inadmissible only under 212(a)(4) upon giving of a suitable bond; the $1,000 minimum is consistent with prior agency practice (except during the 2019 Final Rule period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bonds contemplated but discretionary and case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will exercise bond authority under section 213 of the INA and permit officers, in their discretion, to consider offering public charge bonds to adjustment-of-status applicants inadmissible only under 212(a)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to offer a bond is determined on a case-by-case basis in the exercise of discretion; accepting a bond does not change the underlying standards for inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach determination triggers for bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense would result in a breach determination under the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures public charge bonds achieve their purpose of protecting Federal, State, local, and tribal governments from financial impacts of bonded immigrants becoming public charges.
